## What dapagliflozin is

Dapagliflozin is an **SGLT2 inhibitor**. It blocks SGLT2, a protein in the kidney that normally takes sugar back into the blood, so sugar, salt and water leave the body in the urine instead. The dose is one 10 mg tablet a day.

This module is built on the **SmPC** (summary of product characteristics, the regulator-approved reference text for prescribers) for Forxiga 5 mg and 10 mg. Forxiga is authorised across the whole EU through the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and AstraZeneca AB is the marketing authorisation holder. The version used is the product information the EMA published on 12 March 2026.

## Three different uses

Dapagliflozin started as a diabetes medicine. It is now approved for three conditions:

- **Type 2 diabetes**, in adults and children aged 10 and over, alongside diet and exercise. It can be used on its own when metformin isn't tolerated, or added to other diabetes medicines.
- **Heart failure**, a condition in which the heart doesn't pump blood as well as it should. The indication covers adults with symptoms of long-term heart failure.
- **Chronic kidney disease**, in which the kidneys gradually lose their ability to filter the blood. The indication covers adults.

The heart-failure and kidney uses don't require diabetes.

## What it does to blood sugar

In diabetes, its effect is measured with **HbA1c**, a blood test that reflects average blood sugar over the past two to three months.

- On its own, dapagliflozin lowered HbA1c by 0.66 percentage points more than placebo at 24 weeks.
- Added to other diabetes medicines, the extra reduction was about 0.5 to 0.7 points.
- Against glipizide (a sulphonylurea), both added to metformin, HbA1c fell by 0.52 points with each drug at 52 weeks. That met the trial's test for **non-inferiority**, which shows a new treatment isn't meaningfully worse than an established one.
- In the glipizide comparison, hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) occurred in 3.5% of people on dapagliflozin and 40.8% on glipizide. Body weight fell by 3.2 kg on dapagliflozin and rose by 1.4 kg on glipizide.

## What it does to the heart and kidneys

Some of the results below are given per 100 **patient-years**. One patient-year is one person followed for one year, so rates stay comparable when people are followed for different lengths of time.

- **Heart failure with reduced pumping (DAPA-HF):** 4,744 people, median 18 months. Death from heart causes, hospitalisation for heart failure or an urgent heart-failure visit occurred at 11.6 vs 15.6 per 100 patient-years. That is 26% lower in relative terms and 4 fewer events per 100 patient-years in absolute terms.
- **Heart failure with pumping above 40% (DELIVER):** 6,263 people, median 28 months. 7.8 vs 9.6 per 100 patient-years: 18% lower, and 1.8 fewer per 100 patient-years.
- **Chronic kidney disease (DAPA-CKD):** 4,304 people, median 28.5 months. 9.2% vs 14.5% reached the main outcome, which combined serious kidney decline and death. That is 39% lower in relative terms and 5.3 percentage points lower in absolute terms. The trial was stopped early because the benefit was clear.
- **Type 2 diabetes (DECLARE):** 17,160 people, median 4.2 years. Dapagliflozin didn't reduce heart attack, stroke and heart death combined, but it did no harm on that measure. Hospitalisation for heart failure or heart death was 4.9% vs 5.8%.

## What to watch

- **Genital infections** were the most common side effect, in 5.5% of people vs 0.6% on placebo.
- **Urinary infections** occurred in 4.7% vs 3.5%.
- **Volume depletion**, meaning the body has lost too much fluid, can cause dizziness or low blood pressure.
- **Diabetic ketoacidosis** is a dangerous build-up of acids in the blood. With this medicine it can happen even when blood sugar isn't very high.
- **Fournier's gangrene** is a rare but serious infection of the tissue around the genitals.
- Low blood sugar mainly occurs when dapagliflozin is combined with a sulphonylurea or insulin.

The only contraindication is allergy to the medicine. It shouldn't be used in type 1 diabetes.

## What this module is, and isn't

This is a learning module, not prescribing advice. It is refreshed every six months, or immediately if the SmPC changes or a **safety signal** (new evidence of a possible side effect) appears.

One detail from the start: the SmPC gives no revision date of its own, so this module is dated by the EMA's publication date. The SmPC also gives the first authorisation as 12 November 2012, while the EMA's web page says 11 November.

## Sugar the kidneys usually keep

The kidneys filter sugar out of the blood all the time and then take almost all of it back. Most of that recovery happens in the **proximal tubule**, the first stretch of the kidney's tiny tubes, and SGLT2 does most of the work.

When dapagliflozin blocks SGLT2, the sugar stays in the urine. In people with type 2 diabetes, about 70 g of sugar a day leaves the body this way at the 10 mg dose. That's roughly 280 kilocalories.

## Precise, and independent of insulin

Dapagliflozin is more than 1,400 times more selective for SGLT2 than for **SGLT1**, the main sugar transporter in the gut. So it doesn't block sugar absorption from food.

It works without needing insulin. How much sugar it removes depends on how much is in the blood: when blood sugar is normal, little is removed. That's why it rarely causes low blood sugar on its own, and the body's normal defences against low blood sugar keep working.

## Salt, water and pressure

SGLT2 carries sodium along with sugar, so blocking it keeps salt in the urine too. The sugar also pulls water with it, which is called **osmotic diuresis**. In trials, urine volume went up by about 375 mL a day.

The extra salt reaching further down the kidney's tubes triggers **tubuloglomerular feedback**, a signal that narrows the blood vessel feeding each filter. That lowers **intraglomerular pressure**, the pressure inside the kidney's filters. The SmPC links this, together with less fluid overload and lower blood pressure, to protection of the heart and kidneys, and it says these benefits don't depend only on lowering blood sugar.

## Other measurable changes

At 24 weeks, blood pressure fell by 3.7/1.8 mmHg on dapagliflozin, compared with 0.5/0.5 mmHg on placebo. Weight went down and uric acid fell.

**Haematocrit**, the share of the blood made up of red cells, rose by 2.3 percentage points. This happens because the blood holds less water. These are all markers: they show what the medicine does to the body's chemistry, not what happens to the patient.

## What happens in the body

Blood levels peak within two hours on an empty stomach. **Bioavailability** (the share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream) is 78%. A fatty meal lowers the peak level by up to half but doesn't change the total amount absorbed, so the tablet can be taken with or without food.

The liver and kidneys convert dapagliflozin into an inactive form using an enzyme called **UGT1A9**. The CYP enzymes play only a minor role. The **half-life** (the time it takes for blood levels to fall by half) is about 13 hours, and less than 2% leaves the body unchanged in the urine.

## Kidney function changes the effect more than the exposure

As kidney function falls, blood levels of dapagliflozin rise by 32%, 60% and 87% in mild, moderate and severe impairment. Yet the amount of sugar removed falls sharply: 85 g a day with normal kidneys, then 52, 18 and 11 g.

So the dose doesn't change with kidney function, but the effect on blood sugar fades. Severe liver impairment raises exposure by about two-thirds, which is why a 5 mg starting dose is advised there.

## Few interactions

- Rifampicin lowered dapagliflozin exposure by 22%, and mefenamic acid raised it by 55%. Neither needed a dose change.
- Dapagliflozin didn't meaningfully change levels of metformin, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, glimepiride, hydrochlorothiazide, bumetanide, valsartan, digoxin or warfarin.
- Three interactions do need attention:
  - it adds to the effect of diuretics
  - it can lower lithium levels
  - with insulin or a sulphonylurea, it raises the risk of low blood sugar

One lab test, the 1,5-anhydroglucitol assay, becomes unreliable for tracking blood sugar.

More salt reaching the distal tubule signals the kidney to lower pressure in its filters. This is one proposed route for kidney protection.

## A diabetes medicine first

Dapagliflozin was developed through the diabetes alliance between Bristol-Myers Squibb and AstraZeneca. In the EU it went through the **centralised procedure**, a single EMA assessment that produces one licence valid in every member state. The EU licence was granted in November 2012.

Because of that route, Forxiga has an **EPAR** (European public assessment report, the EMA's published evaluation) and a long list of later assessments. In the US, the FDA approved dapagliflozin as Farxiga in January 2014.

## Outcome trials begin

The first licence covered type 2 diabetes only. DECLARE, a trial in more than 17,000 people designed to check the medicine's effect on heart events, began enrolling in April 2013.

No one could have predicted that dapagliflozin's future would lie as much in heart failure and kidney disease as in blood sugar.

## Class-wide safety reviews

In 2016 and 2017, the EMA ran two **Article 20 referrals**. This is the EU procedure for reviewing a safety concern about centrally authorised medicines, and both reviews covered all SGLT2 inhibitors. The first was about diabetic ketoacidosis. The second was about lower-limb amputations, a concern first raised with canagliflozin.

Both reviews led to warnings that are still in the SmPC today. Lesson 13 covers them in detail.

## Type 1 diabetes: approved in 2019

In early 2019, the EMA announced the first oral medicine to be added to insulin for certain people with type 1 diabetes. This was dapagliflozin 5 mg, for adults with a BMI of 27 or more whose blood sugar wasn't controlled by optimal insulin therapy. The European Commission approved it in March 2019.

The US FDA declined the same use in July 2019.

## From diabetes to heart and kidneys

The large outcome trials then reshaped the licence. Through a series of changes assessed between 2020 and 2022, Forxiga gained indications for heart failure with reduced pumping (based on DAPA-HF) and for chronic kidney disease (based on DAPA-CKD). The heart-failure indication was then extended to people whose heart pumps above 40% (based on DELIVER). Use in type 2 diabetes was also extended to children aged 10 and over.

Today's indications for heart failure and kidney disease don't require diabetes.

## Type 1 diabetes: withdrawn in 2021

On 25 October 2021, AstraZeneca removed the type 1 diabetes indication across the EU and the UK. Regulators stressed that this wasn't because of any new safety concern. In the type 1 trials, diabetic ketoacidosis had been common, affecting at least 1 person in 100. The company pointed to possible confusion now that the medicine was used so widely for other conditions.

The **additional risk minimisation measures**, extra safety materials for doctors and patients beyond the label, were discontinued. Patients were advised to stop in consultation with a diabetes specialist. The UK regulator added that blood pressure may rise slightly after stopping.

A patient organisation, JDRF, estimated that more than 2,000 people were affected.

## Type 2 diabetes: the wording

Forxiga is approved for adults and children aged 10 and over whose type 2 diabetes isn't controlled well enough. In every case it's an **adjunct**: it's added to diet and exercise, never used instead of them.

It can be used in two ways:

- As **monotherapy**, meaning the only diabetes medicine, when metformin is considered inappropriate *due to intolerance*. Compare Januvia, which allows monotherapy for contraindications as well as intolerance.
- Added to other medicines for type 2 diabetes.

## An open-ended partner list

Januvia's licence names each partner medicine it can be combined with. Forxiga's doesn't. It simply says 'in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of type 2 diabetes', and points to sections 4.4, 4.5 and 5.1 for the combinations that were actually studied.

Those studied combinations are:

- metformin
- a sulphonylurea
- metformin plus a sulphonylurea
- sitagliptin, with or without metformin
- insulin
- exenatide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist)
- metformin, when both are started together

Lesson 9 covers each of them.

## Heart failure: no pumping limit in the wording

The heart-failure indication covers adults with symptoms of long-term (chronic) heart failure. It sets no limit on **ejection fraction**, the share of blood the heart pumps out with each beat.

The two trials behind it split patients at that point:

- DAPA-HF: ejection fraction 40% or below
- DELIVER: ejection fraction above 40%

The SmPC flags two gaps. Experience in **NYHA class** IV is limited (NYHA is a I–IV scale of how much heart failure limits daily activity, and IV is the most severe). People with infiltrative cardiomyopathy, a group of diseases in which abnormal material builds up in the heart muscle, weren't studied.

## Chronic kidney disease: broad wording, narrower evidence

The kidney indication simply says 'chronic kidney disease' in adults. The trial behind it, DAPA-CKD, was narrower. It enrolled people with eGFR 25–75 and **albuminuria**, meaning the protein albumin was leaking into the urine (a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 200 to 5,000 mg/g). Two-thirds of the participants had type 2 diabetes.

The SmPC states the gap directly: there is no experience in people who have neither diabetes nor albuminuria. It adds that patients with albuminuria may benefit more. Treatment also shouldn't be *started* below GFR 25.

## Notice what isn't there

- **Type 1 diabetes.** The indication was withdrawn in 2021, and the SmPC now says dapagliflozin 'should not be used' in type 1 diabetes.
- **Children with heart failure or kidney disease.** The EMA waived paediatric studies for these uses, so under-18s aren't covered.

The type 2 diabetes indication does cover children from age 10, but the evidence is modest. The paediatric trial included 72 patients aged 10–24. Its confidence intervals crossed zero, both overall (−0.75 points, 95% CI −1.65 to 0.15) and for under-18s (−0.59, 95% CI −1.66 to 0.48). The label still extends to age 10, partly because children's pharmacokinetics were similar to adults'. Read that as an uncertainty in the label.

## The tablets

Forxiga comes as yellow **film-coated tablets** (tablets with a thin outer layer):

- 5 mg: round, engraved '5' and '1427'
- 10 mg: diamond-shaped, engraved '10' and '1428'

The key **excipient** (an ingredient other than the active substance) is lactose: 25 mg in the 5 mg tablet and 50 mg in the 10 mg tablet. The tablets keep for three years and need no special storage. Packs come as calendar blisters marked Monday to Sunday (14, 28 or 98 tablets), or as unit-dose strips.

## Who stands behind it

The **MAH** (marketing authorisation holder, the company legally responsible for the product) is AstraZeneca AB in Södertälje, Sweden. Batches are released from Södertälje and from Macclesfield in the UK. Because the authorisation is central, every EU country uses the same SmPC, translated into its own language.

## Same medicine, other names

In 2019 the EMA assessed four products together: Forxiga and Edistride (dapagliflozin alone), and Xigduo and Ebymect (dapagliflozin with metformin). Edistride and Ebymect are a **duplicate marketing authorisation**: a second licence for the same product under another brand name. This module hasn't checked whether each duplicate is still marketed.

## Combination tablets

Two **fixed-dose combinations** (two medicines in one tablet) contain dapagliflozin:

- **Xigduo** (also sold as Ebymect): dapagliflozin 5 mg with metformin 850 mg or 1,000 mg, taken twice a day with a meal. It's for people not controlled on metformin alone, as an add-on to other diabetes medicines, or to replace the two taken as separate tablets.
- **Qtern**: saxagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor) with dapagliflozin. It's for adults not controlled on metformin and/or a sulphonylurea plus one of its two components, or already taking both separately.

Lesson 9 looks at the trials behind both.

## Generics

Generic dapagliflozin is now also authorised centrally. For example, Dapagliflozin Viatris showed **bioequivalence** with Forxiga: its blood levels matched closely enough to count as the same medicine. The EMA concluded that, as with Forxiga, its benefits outweigh its risks.

## The routine

The dose is one 10 mg tablet a day, for all three indications. It can be taken at any time of day, with or without food. The tablet is swallowed whole with half a glass of water. The PIL suggests taking it at the same time each day, to make it easier to remember.

When dapagliflozin is added to insulin or a sulphonylurea, the SmPC says a lower dose of that medicine may be considered, to reduce the risk of low blood sugar.

## A missed dose: the 12-hour rule

The PIL gives a precise rule:

- If the next dose is **12 hours or more** away, take the missed tablet as soon as you remember.
- If it's **less than 12 hours** away, skip the missed tablet.

Either way, never take a double dose.

## Kidneys: no dose change, but a starting limit

The dose never changes with kidney function. What changes is when treatment can start and what it achieves:

- Below GFR 25, starting treatment isn't recommended, because experience is limited. In DAPA-CKD, people who were already on treatment continued below 25, and even onto dialysis.
- In type 2 diabetes, the effect on blood sugar is weaker below GFR 45 and probably absent in severe impairment. Extra glucose-lowering treatment may be needed.

Expect an **eGFR dip**, a small, expected fall in kidney function in the first weeks. In DAPA-CKD, eGFR fell by 4.0 on dapagliflozin versus 0.8 on placebo at day 14. By 28 months the overall decline was smaller on dapagliflozin: 7.4 versus 8.6.

## Liver

Mild or moderate liver impairment needs no dose change. In severe impairment, exposure rises by about two-thirds, so the SmPC recommends starting at 5 mg and moving up to 10 mg if the lower dose causes no problems.

## Sick days and surgery

The SmPC sets out a **sick-day rule**, a temporary pause during acute illness:

- **Major surgery or serious acute illness:** interrupt treatment and monitor ketones, preferably in the blood rather than the urine. Restart when ketones are normal and the person is stable.
- **Fluid loss, for example from vomiting or diarrhoea:** pause until the fluid loss is corrected.
- **Serious kidney infection or urosepsis:** consider a pause.

The PIL puts it simply: if you can't eat or drink, or you're vomiting or have a fever, your doctor may ask you to stop until you recover.

## Special groups

- **Older people:** no dose change based on age, but they're more at risk of fluid loss and more often take diuretics.
- **Children:** from age 10 for type 2 diabetes only.
- **Pregnancy:** not recommended in the second and third trimesters, because rat studies showed kidney effects in the young. Stop when a pregnancy is detected.
- **Breastfeeding:** don't use it.
- **Driving:** no meaningful effect on its own, but low blood sugar is possible when it's taken with a sulphonylurea or insulin.

## Overdose and lab tests

Single doses of up to 500 mg caused no toxicity in healthy volunteers, although sugar stayed in their urine for at least five days. Treatment of an overdose is supportive, and it isn't known whether haemodialysis removes dapagliflozin.

Two lab effects are expected. Urine tests will always show sugar, and the 1,5-anhydroglucitol blood test becomes unreliable for judging blood-sugar control.

## Why this lesson comes first

Dapagliflozin's big trials use methods that the earlier modules only touched on: two main questions in one trial, strict rules on which questions can be tested, recurrent events, patient-reported symptoms and pooled trials. This lesson covers each of them before Lesson 8 applies them.

## Two main questions, one strict order

DECLARE had **dual primary endpoints**, meaning two main questions answered at the same time. One was heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death. The other was hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death.

The trial used **hierarchical testing**: questions are tested in a fixed order, and testing stops at the first question that fails. Superiority on heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death wasn't shown (p = 0.172). So the next questions, on kidney outcomes and death from any cause, weren't formally tested. Their p-values are reported as **nominal**: calculated, but not protected against chance findings.

## Look inside the composite

A **composite endpoint** counts several kinds of event together, so always check which part drives the result.

In DECLARE, the heart-failure-or-death composite improved (HR 0.83). That came almost entirely from fewer hospitalisations for heart failure (HR 0.73), not from fewer deaths (HR 0.98).

DAPA-HF and DELIVER also counted urgent heart-failure visits, which are softer events than death. DAPA-HF reports that all three parts contributed, and that urgent visits were few.

## Stating effects honestly

In DAPA-HF, the main outcome occurred at 11.6 events per 100 patient-years on dapagliflozin versus 15.6 on placebo. That is about 4 fewer events per 100 patient-years in absolute terms. The hazard ratio of 0.74 means about 26% fewer in relative terms.

Every trial in this module is reported with both kinds of figure, together with what it was compared against and over what time.

## First events and all events

Most trials count only each person's *first* event. But heart failure keeps coming back. A **rate ratio** compares *all* events, first and repeat, between groups.

In DAPA-HF, there were 567 heart-failure hospitalisations and cardiovascular deaths on dapagliflozin and 742 on placebo, a rate ratio of 0.75. That's close to the first-event result, which suggests the benefit continues beyond the first event.

## How patients feel

A **patient-reported outcome** is a measure scored by patients themselves. Heart-failure trials use the KCCQ questionnaire, which measures symptoms on a 0–100 scale.

The result can be expressed as a **win ratio**. Each patient on the drug is compared with each patient on placebo, and every pair is scored as a win, a loss or a tie. A win ratio above 1 favours the drug: 1.18 in DAPA-HF and 1.11 in DELIVER.

## When a trial stops early

DAPA-CKD was stopped early for efficacy, on the advice of its independent **data monitoring committee**, the group that reviews results while a trial is still running.

As with rosuvastatin's JUPITER trial, stopping at a moment of clear benefit can overstate how large the effect really is. The direction is reliable, but treat the size with some caution.

## Subgroups and pooled trials

DAPA-HF and DAPA-CKD each checked a subgroup planned in advance: patients with and without diabetes. The effect was similar in both.

A **pooled analysis** combines individual patients' data from several trials. Pooling DAPA-HF and DELIVER, as planned in advance, showed fewer cardiovascular deaths (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.75–0.96), a result that neither trial showed clearly on its own.

## Not worse, as well as better

The glipizide comparison tested non-inferiority. At 52 weeks, the HbA1c difference was 0.00 points, with a 95% CI of −0.11 to 0.11, well inside the trial's margin.

DECLARE tested non-inferiority on heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death first, and passed (one-sided p < 0.001). Only after that did it test superiority, which it didn't show.

## The combination tags

Each trial card carries exactly one tag for the background therapy:

- MONO: no background glucose-lowering medicine
- 🔗 +MET: metformin
- 🔗 +MET+SU: metformin plus a sulphonylurea
- 🔗 +DPP4: a DPP-4 inhibitor, with or without metformin
- 🔗 +SU: a sulphonylurea
- 🔗 +INSULIN: insulin
- 🔗 +GLP1: a GLP-1 receptor agonist
- 🔗 +STATIN: a statin
- 🔗 +ANTIHTN: blood-pressure medicines, including ACE inhibitors or ARBs
- 🔗 +HF-SOC: standard heart-failure treatment
- 🔗 FDC: a fixed-dose combination tablet
- 🔗 MIXED: usual care that varied between patients

## Reading a card

Every card has eight lines: registry number, who took part, background therapy, what the drug was compared with, the main question, the headline result, what it means in plain words, and what's worth knowing.

The **registry number** points to the trial's public record.

## Four outcome trials and one glucose trial

Forxiga's three indications rest on four large **pivotal trials**, the trials that regulators relied on: DECLARE for diabetes, DAPA-HF and DELIVER for heart failure, and DAPA-CKD for kidney disease. A fifth card shows the head-to-head glucose trial against glipizide.

All four outcome trials compared dapagliflozin 10 mg with placebo, on top of the patient's usual treatment.

### Trial card: DECLARE-TIMI 58
Tag: 🔗 MIXED

- Registry: NCT01730534
- Who took part: 17,160 adults with type 2 diabetes, 40.6% with established cardiovascular disease and 10% with heart failure; mean eGFR 85
- Background therapy: usual diabetes care; 98% were on at least one diabetes medicine (metformin 82%, sulphonylurea 43%, insulin 41%)
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 4.2 years
- Main question: two primary endpoints. (1) Heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death. (2) Hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death.
- Headline result: (1) 8.8% vs 9.4%, HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.84–1.03): non-inferior, but superiority not shown (p = 0.172). (2) 4.9% vs 5.8%, HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.73–0.95), p = 0.005: about 17% lower in relative terms and 0.9 percentage points lower in absolute terms.
- In plain words: dapagliflozin didn't reduce heart attacks or strokes. It did reduce hospitalisation for heart failure (2.5% vs 3.3%), with no change in cardiovascular death (2.9% vs 2.9%).
- Worth knowing: the kidney composite (4.3% vs 5.6%, HR 0.76) and death from any cause (6.2% vs 6.6%, HR 0.93) are nominal only, because hierarchical testing stopped. This trial started the heart-failure story.

### Trial card: DAPA-HF
Tag: 🔗 +HF-SOC

- Registry: NCT03036124
- Who took part: 4,744 adults with heart failure, ejection fraction 40% or below, NYHA class II–IV, and eGFR 30 or above; 42% had type 2 diabetes
- Background therapy: standard heart-failure treatment. 94% took an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI; 96% a beta-blocker; 71% an MRA; 93% a diuretic.
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 18 months
- Main question: does dapagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death, hospitalisation for heart failure or an urgent heart-failure visit?
- Headline result: 11.6 vs 15.6 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85), p < 0.0001. That is about 26% fewer in relative terms and 4 fewer per 100 patient-years in absolute terms.
- In plain words: on top of full heart-failure treatment, dapagliflozin reduced deaths and worsening heart failure, with or without diabetes (HR 0.75 with, 0.73 without).
- Worth knowing: all three parts of the outcome contributed. Total events (first and repeat) fell similarly, with a rate ratio of 0.75. Symptoms improved on the KCCQ questionnaire (win ratio 1.18).

### Trial card: DELIVER
Tag: 🔗 +HF-SOC

- Registry: NCT03619213
- Who took part: 6,263 adults aged 40 or over with heart failure, ejection fraction above 40% and structural heart disease; 10% were enrolled during or soon after a hospital stay; 45% had type 2 diabetes
- Background therapy: standard care. 98% took a diuretic, 83% a beta-blocker, 77% an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI, and 43% an MRA.
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 28 months
- Main question: does dapagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death, hospitalisation for heart failure or an urgent heart-failure visit?
- Headline result: 7.8 vs 9.6 events per 100 patient-years; HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92), p = 0.0008. That is about 18% fewer in relative terms and 1.8 fewer per 100 patient-years in absolute terms.
- In plain words: the benefit extended to people whose hearts still pump reasonably well, across all ejection-fraction bands (49% or below, 50–59%, 60% or above).
- Worth knowing: the effect was smaller than in DAPA-HF, and the patients were older with more mild symptoms. Pooled with DAPA-HF, cardiovascular death was lower (HR 0.85). This trial is why the EU indication has no ejection-fraction limit.

### Trial card: DAPA-CKD
Tag: 🔗 +ANTIHTN

- Registry: NCT03036150
- Who took part: 4,304 adults with chronic kidney disease, eGFR 25–75 and albuminuria (mean eGFR 43); 67.5% had type 2 diabetes
- Background therapy: standard care, with 97% on an ACE inhibitor or ARB
- Compared with: placebo, over a median of 28.5 months, stopped early for efficacy
- Main question: does dapagliflozin reduce a sustained fall in eGFR of at least 50%, kidney failure, or kidney or cardiovascular death?
- Headline result: 9.2% vs 14.5%, about 39% lower in relative terms and 5.3 percentage points lower in absolute terms. The effect was visible from month 4.
- In plain words: dapagliflozin slowed kidney disease and cut deaths, with or without diabetes (HR 0.64 with diabetes, 0.50 without).
- Worth knowing: death from any cause was also significantly lower. Because the trial stopped early, the effect may be overstated. It was also the safety study used to track the class's amputation signal.

### Trial card: dapagliflozin vs glipizide
Tag: 🔗 +MET

- Registry: NCT00660907
- Who took part: 801 adults with type 2 diabetes not controlled on metformin (HbA1c 6.5–10%)
- Background therapy: metformin
- Compared with: glipizide, a sulphonylurea, head-to-head over 52 weeks, with extensions to 208 weeks
- Main question: is dapagliflozin no worse than glipizide at lowering HbA1c?
- Headline result: −0.52 vs −0.52 points at 52 weeks; difference 0.00 (95% CI −0.11 to 0.11), which is non-inferior. Weight changed by −3.2 vs +1.4 kg. Hypoglycaemia occurred in 3.5% vs 40.8%.
- In plain words: blood sugar fell equally, with weight loss instead of weight gain and far less hypoglycaemia.
- Worth knowing: by 208 weeks, HbA1c had drifted to −0.10 vs +0.20. Fewer than 40% of patients remained in the trial by then, so long-term figures rest on a shrinking group.

## Six partner groups

People on dapagliflozin usually take other medicines too. This lesson looks at six situations: dapagliflozin **alone**, with **metformin**, with a **statin**, with a **GLP-1 receptor agonist** (an injected diabetes medicine that mimics the gut hormone GLP-1), with a **DPP-4 inhibitor**, and with **blood-pressure medicines**.

For each one, it asks three questions: what the licences name, what the SmPC says, and which trials exist.

## What the licences name

- **Forxiga:** open wording, 'in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of type 2 diabetes'. No partner is named.
- **Xigduo and Ebymect:** dapagliflozin and metformin in one tablet.
- **Qtern:** dapagliflozin and saxagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor) in one tablet.

This pass found no EU licence that combines dapagliflozin with a statin, a GLP-1 receptor agonist or a blood-pressure medicine. When those medicines are used together, each is prescribed on its own licence, which is called **co-administration**.

## What the SmPC says about each partner

- **Metformin, sitagliptin, glimepiride, pioglitazone:** no meaningful change in drug levels in either direction.
- **Simvastatin:** a single 20 mg dose of dapagliflozin raised simvastatin exposure by 19% and simvastatin acid by 31%. The SmPC doesn't consider this clinically relevant.
- **Thiazide and loop diuretics:** the water-losing effect adds up, raising the risk of dehydration and low blood pressure.
- **Other blood-pressure medicines:** no change in levels with valsartan. The SmPC asks for caution in people on blood-pressure treatment who have a history of low blood pressure.
- **Insulin and sulphonylureas:** a lower dose may be needed to avoid hypoglycaemia.
- **GLP-1 receptor agonists:** there is no interaction line. The only data are the exenatide trial described in section 5.1.

Each column comes from different trials. They differ in how long they ran, where patients' HbA1c started (7.7% to 9.3%) and who took part. The biggest reductions, about 2 points, come from trials where patients started with a high HbA1c, above 9%. ### Trial card: DURATION-8 (with exenatide)
Tag: 🔗 +MET

- Registry: NCT02229396
- Who took part: 685 adults with type 2 diabetes not controlled on metformin, HbA1c 8–12% (average about 9.3%)
- Background therapy: metformin
- Compared with: dapagliflozin alone and once-weekly exenatide alone, over 28 weeks, double-blind
- Main question: does dapagliflozin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist lower HbA1c more than either medicine alone?
- Headline result: HbA1c fell 1.98 points with the combination, 1.39 with dapagliflozin and 1.60 with exenatide. The combination did 0.59 points better than dapagliflozin and 0.38 better than exenatide. Weight fell 3.6 kg vs 2.2 and 1.6 kg.
- In plain words: the two classes add up. Blood sugar, weight and systolic blood pressure (−4.3 vs −1.8 and −1.2 mmHg) all improved more with the combination.
- Worth knowing: this is the only trial of a dapagliflozin plus GLP-1 receptor agonist combination in the SmPC. It measured glucose, weight and blood pressure, not heart or kidney outcomes. Exenatide is one GLP-1 receptor agonist; others weren't studied here.

### Trial card: added to sitagliptin
Tag: 🔗 +DPP4

- Registry: NCT00984867
- Who took part: 447 adults not controlled on sitagliptin 100 mg, with or without metformin
- Background therapy: sitagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor), with or without metformin
- Compared with: placebo added, over 24 weeks with an extension to 48 weeks
- Main question: does adding dapagliflozin to a DPP-4 inhibitor lower HbA1c?
- Headline result: HbA1c fell 0.48 points more than with placebo at 24 weeks (95% CI −0.62 to −0.34). At 48 weeks it was −0.30 vs +0.38, and weight was 2.2 kg lower.
- In plain words: dapagliflozin added real glucose lowering on top of sitagliptin, and the effect lasted.
- Worth knowing: hypoglycaemia stayed below 5%, similar to placebo. This is the same trial that appears in the sitagliptin module, seen from the other side. The licensed single-tablet pairing uses saxagliptin (Qtern), not sitagliptin.

### Trial card: starting dapagliflozin and metformin together
Tag: MONO

- Registry: NCT00643851 and NCT00859898
- Who took part: adults with type 2 diabetes not on any medicine, HbA1c 7.5–12% (average about 9.0%); 1,236 patients across two studies
- Background therapy: none. Both medicines were started at the same time.
- Compared with: dapagliflozin alone and metformin alone, over 24 weeks
- Main question: does starting both medicines together lower HbA1c more than either alone?
- Headline result: HbA1c fell 1.98 points with the combination (211 patients), 1.45 with dapagliflozin and 1.44 with metformin. The combination did about 0.5 points better than either alone.
- In plain words: starting both together worked better than starting one.
- Worth knowing: dapagliflozin alone matched metformin alone here (difference −0.01). Even so, the licence allows dapagliflozin on its own only when metformin isn't tolerated.

### Trial card: blood-pressure studies on an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Tag: 🔗 +ANTIHTN

- Registry: NCT01137474 and NCT01195662 (two 12-week studies)
- Who took part: 1,062 adults with type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, not controlled despite stable treatment. In one study patients were on an ACE inhibitor or ARB; in the other, on an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus one more blood-pressure medicine.
- Background therapy: an ACE inhibitor or ARB, with or without one more blood-pressure medicine
- Compared with: placebo, over 12 weeks
- Main question: does dapagliflozin lower HbA1c and blood pressure on top of blood-pressure treatment?
- Headline result: systolic blood pressure fell 3.1 and 4.3 mmHg more than with placebo in the two studies. HbA1c also improved; the SmPC doesn't give the figure.
- In plain words: on top of existing blood-pressure medicines, dapagliflozin lowered systolic pressure a few more points.
- Worth knowing: the effect is modest, and it's larger when blood sugar is very high. The SmPC asks for caution when a fall in blood pressure could be risky, for example in older people or those with a history of low blood pressure.

### Trial card: added to insulin
Tag: 🔗 +INSULIN

- Registry: NCT00673231
- Who took part: 387 adults on insulin, half also on one or two oral diabetes medicines
- Background therapy: insulin, with or without oral diabetes medicines
- Compared with: placebo added, over 24 weeks with extensions to 104 weeks
- Main question: does adding dapagliflozin improve control and reduce the insulin dose needed?
- Headline result: HbA1c fell 0.60 points more than with placebo at 24 weeks. The daily insulin dose was 6.2 units lower than with placebo. At 104 weeks, HbA1c was −0.71 vs −0.06.

## Four questions, four answers

- **Heart attacks and strokes:** no reduction (DECLARE).
- **Heart failure:** fewer hospitalisations, in three trials.
- **Kidneys:** slower decline (DAPA-CKD, and nominally in DECLARE).
- **Death:** lower in DAPA-CKD, and cardiovascular death was lower when the two heart-failure trials were pooled.

This lesson unpacks each answer.

## Heart attacks and strokes

In DECLARE (17,160 people with type 2 diabetes, median 4.2 years), dapagliflozin met the test for non-inferiority on the combination of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death. It didn't show superiority: 8.8% vs 9.4%, HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.84–1.03).

The individual events followed the same pattern:

- **Heart attack:** 4.6% vs 5.1% (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.77–1.01)
- **Ischaemic stroke:** 2.7% vs 2.7% (HR 1.01)

These component results are nominal only. There is no claim of fewer heart attacks or strokes.

## Heart failure

Heart failure is where the trials agree most clearly:

- **DECLARE:** hospitalisation for heart failure 2.5% vs 3.3% (HR 0.73). That's about 27% fewer in relative terms and 0.8 percentage points fewer in absolute terms, over 4.2 years. It applied to people with and without existing heart failure.
- **DAPA-HF:** HR 0.74 for the combined outcome.
- **DELIVER:** HR 0.82 for the combined outcome.

Both heart-failure trials also cut the total of first and repeat events (rate ratios 0.75 and 0.77). The benefit was similar in people with and without diabetes.

## Kidneys

- **DAPA-CKD:** the primary kidney outcome occurred in 9.2% vs 14.5%, a confirmed result.
- **DECLARE:** the kidney composite was 4.3% vs 5.6% (HR 0.76). Most of the difference came from fewer sustained falls in eGFR (1.4% vs 2.6%) and fewer cases of end-stage kidney disease (6 vs 19 people). Dapagliflozin also reduced new albuminuria (HR 0.79). Remember that DECLARE's kidney results are nominal only.
- **DAPA-HF:** there were too few kidney events to draw conclusions (1.2% vs 1.6%).

## Death

- **DECLARE:** death from any cause 6.2% vs 6.6% (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82–1.04). Nominal, and not significant. Cardiovascular death was 2.9% in both groups.
- **DAPA-CKD:** death from any cause was significantly reduced. The SmPC shows the size of the effect only in a figure, so it isn't quoted here.
- **DAPA-HF and DELIVER pooled:** cardiovascular death was lower (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.75–0.96, p = 0.0115). Both trials contributed.

The PIL puts it in patients' terms: Forxiga 'can help some patients to live longer'.

## How the SmPC counts

The main safety picture comes from 13 placebo-controlled studies of up to 24 weeks: 2,360 people on dapagliflozin and 2,295 on placebo. More than 15,000 people took it across the type 2 diabetes studies overall.

None of the side effects were dose-related. The most frequent were genital infections.

## By frequency

- **Very common:** hypoglycaemia, but only when taken with a sulphonylurea or insulin
- **Common:** genital and urinary infections, dizziness, rash, back pain, passing urine more often or painfully, higher haematocrit, changes in blood fats, and a temporary drop in kidney clearance early in treatment
- **Uncommon:** fluid loss, thirst, constipation, dry mouth, waking at night to pass urine, genital itching, weight loss
- **Rare:** diabetic ketoacidosis (in type 2 diabetes)
- **Very rare:**
  - Fournier's gangrene
  - angioedema
  - **tubulointerstitial nephritis**, an inflammation of the tissue between the kidney's tubes

## Genital infections

In the study pool, genital infections occurred in 5.5% on dapagliflozin vs 0.6% on placebo, and in women 8.4% vs 1.2%. That's about 5 percentage points more overall, roughly nine times as often. Most were mild to moderate, cleared with standard treatment, and rarely led to stopping. People who'd had them before were more likely to get them again.

The SmPC also reports cases of **phimosis**, a tightening of the foreskin, alongside genital infections. Some of these needed circumcision.

## Urinary infections

In the study pool, urinary infections occurred in 4.7% vs 3.5%. In the big outcome trials, serious urinary infections were fewer in DECLARE (0.9% vs 1.3%) but more frequent in DAPA-CKD (1.3% vs 0.8%).

The SmPC suggests considering a pause in treatment during a kidney infection or urosepsis.

## Ketoacidosis at near-normal sugar

Diabetic ketoacidosis is rare, but with SGLT2 inhibitors it can be **euglycaemic**: blood sugar is only moderately raised, below 14 mmol/L, which makes it easy to miss. It should be suspected when someone has nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, fast breathing, confusion or unusual tiredness, whatever their blood sugar.

In DECLARE, 27 people on dapagliflozin had ketoacidosis vs 12 on placebo, and 22 of the 27 were on insulin. In the heart-failure and kidney trials there were very few cases (5 vs 2 in total).

Ketoacidosis can last longer than the drug's half-life would suggest. The SmPC advises against restarting after an episode, unless a clear trigger has been found and resolved.

## Fournier's gangrene

Fournier's gangrene is a rare, life-threatening infection that destroys tissue in the genital area and needs urgent surgery and antibiotics. Cases have been reported with every SGLT2 inhibitor since they came to market. The warning signs are pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genitals or the area between the genitals and the anus, together with fever or feeling unwell.

In DECLARE there were 6 cases: 1 on dapagliflozin and 5 on placebo. A single trial of this size can't settle a risk this rare, which is why reports collected after launch matter.

## Fluid loss and the kidneys

- **Fluid loss:** 1.1% vs 0.7% in the study pool. In DAPA-HF, serious fluid-loss events were actually *fewer* on dapagliflozin (1.0% vs 1.6%). In DAPA-CKD, any fluid-loss event was more common (5.6% vs 3.9%), but serious events were equal (0.7% vs 0.7%).
- **Kidney numbers:** creatinine-related events were 3.2% vs 1.8%, rising to 18.5% vs 9.3% in people with eGFR 30–60. Most changes were small (44 µmol/L or less) and either temporary or reversible. This is the expected early dip in eGFR.

## Class observations

- **Amputations:** long-term studies of SGLT2 inhibitors found more lower-limb amputations, mainly of toes. It isn't known whether this is a **class effect**, one shared by every drug in the group. The SmPC's advice is routine preventive foot care for people with diabetes.
- **Haematocrit:** values above 55% occurred in 1.3% vs 0.4%. A marked rise should be investigated for a blood disorder.
- **Children:** the safety profile in 10–17-year-olds matched that in adults.

## When to act

The PIL tells patients to contact a doctor straight away if they notice:

- signs of ketoacidosis
- signs of Fournier's gangrene
- swelling of the face, tongue or throat (angioedema)

It tells them to stop taking Forxiga and see a doctor if they have signs of a severe urinary infection: fever or chills, burning when passing urine, or back or side pain. They should also report blood in the urine.

blocks.markdown:
## One contraindication

The only contraindication is allergy to dapagliflozin or to any ingredient of the tablet.

## 'Should not be used' and 'not recommended'

The SmPC tells prescribers to avoid dapagliflozin in several situations that aren't formal contraindications:

- **Type 1 diabetes:** should not be used. Ketoacidosis was common in type 1 trials.
- **Breastfeeding:** should not be used.
- **Pregnancy:** not recommended in the second and third trimesters. Stop if a pregnancy is detected.
- **Starting below GFR 25:** not recommended, because experience is limited.
- **Under-18s with heart failure or kidney disease:** safety and efficacy not established.

These rest on known risks or missing data, not on an absolute ban.

## Who needs extra care

- **Risk of fluid loss or low blood pressure:** older people, people on blood-pressure medicines with a history of low blood pressure, and people with very high blood sugar.
- **Higher risk of ketoacidosis:**
  - people with little insulin of their own, for example low **C-peptide** (a marker of the body's own insulin production)
  - people with **LADA**, a slow-onset autoimmune diabetes in adults
  - people with past pancreatitis
  - people who aren't eating or are dehydrated
  - people whose insulin dose has been cut
  - people whose insulin need has risen through illness, surgery or alcohol
- **Heart failure with NYHA class IV:** experience is limited. Infiltrative cardiomyopathy hasn't been studied.
- **Lactose:** people with rare inherited sugar intolerances shouldn't take it.

## Interactions: effect rather than blood levels

The interactions that matter most change the effect, not the drug's blood levels:

- **Diuretics:** the water-losing effect adds up, raising the risk of dehydration and low blood pressure.
- **Insulin and sulphonylureas:** the risk of hypoglycaemia rises, so consider a lower dose of these.
- **Lithium:** dapagliflozin can lower lithium levels, so they should be checked more often. The lithium prescriber should be involved.

## Interactions: blood levels

Dapagliflozin is broken down mainly by UGT1A9. It neither blocks nor boosts the CYP enzymes, so it isn't expected to change how other drugs are cleared.

- **Rifampicin:** lowers dapagliflozin exposure by 22%. No dose change is needed.
- **Mefenamic acid** (which blocks UGT1A9): raises dapagliflozin exposure by 55%. No dose change is needed.
- **No meaningful change** was seen with metformin, pioglitazone, sitagliptin, glimepiride, voglibose, hydrochlorothiazide, bumetanide, valsartan, simvastatin, digoxin or warfarin. For warfarin, the INR was unchanged too.

All interaction studies were done in adults.

## Watching after approval

**Pharmacovigilance** means monitoring a medicine's safety once it's on the market. The Forxiga SmPC asks healthcare professionals to report suspected side effects through their national system, and the PIL invites patients to report directly.

For dapagliflozin, most of the big safety decisions were made for the whole SGLT2 inhibitor class, not for this one medicine alone.

## 2016: ketoacidosis without very high sugar

In 2016 the EMA completed an EU-wide review of diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors. It found rare cases, some life-threatening, and many were atypical: blood sugar wasn't as high as doctors would expect, which could delay diagnosis. The review made five recommendations:

- Stop immediately if ketoacidosis is suspected, and don't restart unless another cause has been found and resolved.
- Use caution when risk factors are present: low insulin reserve, a sudden cut in insulin dose, illness, surgery, alcohol misuse, poor intake or dehydration.
- Pause treatment for major surgery or a hospital stay with serious illness.
- Remember that SGLT2 inhibitors weren't authorised for type 1 diabetes.
- The benefits still outweigh the risks.

Every one of these points is in today's SmPC.

## 2016–2017: the amputation question

In March 2016, the CANVAS trial of canagliflozin, another SGLT2 inhibitor, showed about twice as many lower-limb amputations as placebo, mostly of toes. The European Commission started an **Article 20 procedure**, an EU-wide safety review. In July 2016, because all SGLT2 inhibitors share the same mechanism and a class effect couldn't be ruled out, the review was widened to the whole class.

In February 2017 the EMA's safety committee, the **PRAC**, concluded that no increased risk had been seen with dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. However, the data were limited, so the risk might still apply to them. Every SGLT2 inhibitor now carries a warning about foot care. The dapagliflozin SmPC still says it is 'unknown whether this constitutes a class effect'.

## A kidney trial that was also a safety study

DAPA-CKD had a second job. In the risk management plan, it was listed as a **post-authorisation safety study** (PASS), meaning a study required after approval to check a specific risk. Here, that risk was amputation.

So the trial that won the kidney indication was also collecting evidence on the class's amputation question.

## 2021: a safety letter to end an indication

When the type 1 diabetes indication was withdrawn in 2021, prescribers were informed by a direct healthcare professional communication (DHPC), a safety letter agreed with the regulator. It explained four points:

- The 5 mg dose should no longer be used for type 1 diabetes.
- The withdrawal wasn't due to a new safety concern.
- Diabetic ketoacidosis had been common in the type 1 trials.
- Patients should stop in consultation with a specialist.

The extra safety materials that had supported the type 1 indication were discontinued.

## Regular check-ups and the risk plan

The EPAR lists periodic safety update single assessments (PSUSAs) for dapagliflozin from 2017, 2022 and 2024. Their outcomes haven't been read for this module yet. The risk management plan was last updated in June 2026.

One point to note: the SmPC's list of side effects already includes items added after the medicine was launched, such as Fournier's gangrene, angioedema and tubulointerstitial nephritis.

## What triggers a refresh

- Updated Forxiga product information from the EMA
- A PSUSA that ends in a label change
- A PRAC signal on SGLT2 inhibitors

The current basis is the product information published on 12 March 2026. The items to watch are amputation (still an open class question) and ketoacidosis around surgery and illness.

lessons.title: Where the ESC guidelines place it

blocks.markdown:
## Three guidelines, one medicine

Dapagliflozin has three indications, and three ESC guidelines cover them: heart failure, diabetes with cardiovascular disease, and (through both) kidney disease. Guidelines advise on practice; they don't change the licence.

Each recommendation has a **class of recommendation** (I means 'is recommended') and a **level of evidence** (A means several randomised trials).

## Heart failure with reduced pumping

The 2021 ESC heart-failure guideline built its treatment plan for reduced ejection fraction on **four pillars**: the four drug classes that every suitable patient should receive:

- an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI
- a beta-blocker
- a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
- an SGLT2 inhibitor, dapagliflozin or empagliflozin

DAPA-HF is the trial behind dapagliflozin's place among them.

## Heart failure with better pumping

The 2023 focused update extended the recommendation. Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin is now **recommended (Class I, level A)** in heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (41–49%) and in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (50% or above). The goal is to reduce heart-failure hospitalisation or cardiovascular death.

That makes SGLT2 inhibitors, along with diuretics for fluid, the only Class I drugs in those groups. The other pillars stay at the weaker Class IIb in mildly reduced ejection fraction, and have no specific recommendation in preserved ejection fraction. DELIVER, and empagliflozin's EMPEROR-Preserved, are the trials behind the change.

## Diabetes and kidney disease

The same 2023 update recommends dapagliflozin or empagliflozin (Class I, level A) for people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, to reduce heart-failure hospitalisation or cardiovascular death.

The 2023 ESC diabetes guideline recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or a GLP-1 receptor agonist in type 2 diabetes with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, whatever the blood sugar. It also recommends SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure.

Here the label and the guidelines match closely, unlike the sitagliptin module, where the label lagged behind practice. Both drop the ejection-fraction split for SGLT2 inhibitors, and both place the heart and kidney uses outside a pure blood-sugar logic.

## Dapagliflozin on one page

*Basis: Forxiga EU SmPC, product information published by the EMA on 12 March 2026. Next refresh: March 2027.*

**What it is.** An SGLT2 inhibitor. It blocks sugar and salt reabsorption in the kidney, and about 70 g of sugar a day leaves in the urine. It works independently of insulin. Its heart and kidney effects work through salt, water and pressure, not only through blood sugar.

**What it's approved for.** Type 2 diabetes (from age 10), symptomatic chronic heart failure at any ejection fraction, and chronic kidney disease in adults. The heart and kidney uses don't require diabetes. Type 1 diabetes was approved in 2019 and withdrawn in 2021.

**How it's taken.** 10 mg once a day for all indications, with or without food. There's no dose change for kidney function, but don't start below GFR 25. Start at 5 mg in severe liver impairment. Pause for surgery or acute illness.

**What it does.**
- Blood sugar: about −0.5 to −0.7 points added to other medicines. The effect fades below GFR 45.
- Diabetes (DECLARE): no effect on heart attacks or strokes. Fewer heart-failure hospitalisations: 2.5% vs 3.3%.
- Heart failure: HR 0.74 (DAPA-HF) and HR 0.82 (DELIVER). Pooled cardiovascular death HR 0.85.
- Kidneys (DAPA-CKD): 9.2% vs 14.5%, with and without diabetes, and fewer deaths.

**Safety.** Genital infections (5.5% vs 0.6%). Ketoacidosis, including with near-normal blood sugar. Fournier's gangrene (very rare). Volume depletion. A small, expected early dip in eGFR. Class warnings from EU reviews on ketoacidosis (2016) and amputation (2017). The only contraindication is allergy.

**Combinations.** Licensed tablets with metformin (Xigduo) and with saxagliptin (Qtern). It adds to exenatide, sitagliptin and blood-pressure medicines. There's no statin combination licence; a phase 3 single-tablet trial with rosuvastatin is under way.

**Guidelines.** One of four pillars in reduced ejection fraction. ESC Class I A above 40% ejection fraction, and in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease.
